newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Novartis set to become world's generic drug leader.
newsitem.headline: Novartis set to become world's generic drug leader.

text.p: Sandoz AG's purchase of Azupharma GmbH, Germany's third-largest generic drugs company, underscores Novartis Inc's strategy to be world leader in the fast-growing generics business, Sandoz said.

Sandoz -- whose mega-merger with Ciba-Geigy AG will create Novartis -- will pay Gehe AG 640 million marks ($416.2 million) for Azupharma, giving the Swiss company its first foothold in the German generics market, the second biggest in the world.
"The acquisition will lift Sandoz's generic business -- already strong with its affiliate Biochemie, Kundl -- to a front-runner position worldwide," it said in a statement.

The acquisition also fits well with the strategy of Novartis. Combined with Azupharm, the companies' total generics turnover would amount to some 1.4 billion Swiss francs a year, a company spokesman said.
"The worldwide demand for generic pharmaceuticals is growing rapidly at a rate of nearly 11 percent per annum," Daniel Vasella, the designated chief executive of Novartis, said in a statement.

"The firm foothold we have in this market today will be strengthened further by Azupharma. We intend to expand our position as a leading player in generics, to serve large customers with a full product range and to maximise the life-cycle management of out mature products."
Based in Gerlingen near Stuttgart, Azupharma employs 440 people and generated sales of 222 million marks in 1995. Branded generics account for 80 percent of sales.

Generics -- cut-rate drugs that compete against rivals whose patents have expired -- are set to grow in importance in Germany, driven by the national reference price system and pressure on prescribers to limit medicine budgets, Sandoz said.

"Azupharma's strong position in Germany will provide a channel for Sandoz to penetrate the market further and will broaden Novartis' strategic platform for launching generics when patent protection expires," it said.
Although margins on generics are routinely narrower than on sspecialised products, they can still be profitable, the spokesman said.
"If it is well managed, you can reach margins that we think are decent for Novartis," he said.
